lead: The poles of a system decide how fast it settles and how much it overshoots. In state space you can move those poles to chosen positions, provided the system is controllable. Measure every state, multiply the state vector by a gain row K, and subtract it from the reference: u = r − Kx. The closed-loop matrix becomes A − BK, and its eigenvalues are the new poles. Aircraft autopilots, servo drives and inverted-pendulum rigs use this when a fast, well-damped response is demanded and the states are already on the sensor list.
prereq: You need: Chapter 6.4 for the controllability test, Chapter 6.1 for the state model, and Unit 3, Stability and Root Locus, for deciding where the poles should sit.

sections.h3: Close the loop around every state

blocks.text: Output feedback in Unit 5 uses one signal y and one gain. State feedback uses the whole state vector x, an n × 1 column of measured variables, and a gain matrix K. For a single input, K is a 1 × n row of numbers. The control law is u = r − Kx: the scalar input u is the reference r minus the weighted sum Kx of all the states.
Put this law into the state equation x' = Ax + Bu:
x' = Ax + B(r − Kx) = (A − BK)x + Br
blocks.where: x is the n × 1 state vector; A is the n × n plant matrix; B is the n × 1 input matrix; K is the 1 × n gain row; r is the scalar reference; A − BK is the closed-loop matrix; Br acts as the input to the closed loop.

blocks.text: The closed-loop poles are the eigenvalues of A − BK, that is the roots of det(sI − (A − BK)) = 0. Eigenvalues fix the decay rates and the damping, as Chapter 6.3 shows. Choose K and you choose those roots. This is pole placement, also called pole assignment.

Root locus design (Unit 3) also moves poles, but a single scalar gain slides them along fixed paths. K carries n independent numbers, one per state, so all n poles can be steered to chosen places — provided the pair (A, B) is controllable.
For a single-input system with n states the design is pure algebra, done in five steps.

items: Test controllability: the matrix Qc = [B AB A²B … An−1B] must have rank n (Chapter 6.4). If it does not, stop; no K exists.

Write the desired polynomial from the target poles p<sub>1</sub> to p<sub>n</sub>: φ(s) = (s − p<sub>1</sub>)(s − p<sub>2</sub>) … (s − p<sub>n</sub>) = s<sup>n</sup> + a<sub>n−1</sub>s<sup>n−1</sup> + … + a<sub>0</sub>. For a stable design every p<sub>i</sub> has a negative real part.
Write A − BK with the gains k<sub>1</sub>, k<sub>2</sub>, …, k<sub>n</sub> left as unknowns.
Expand det(sI − (A − BK)) and collect powers of s. Each coefficient is a straight-line expression in the k<sub>i</sub>.
Equate coefficients with φ(s) from the highest power down. The n linear equations give the n gains.

blocks.text: The coefficient equations are linear, so they have a unique solution exactly when the system is controllable. Complex target poles are allowed; they must appear in conjugate pairs so that K stays real. Placing poles far to the left gives a fast loop but needs large gains and large control effort, which real actuators may not supply.
Matching coefficients by hand is fine for two or three states. For a larger single-input system, one matrix formula does the whole job.

blocks.where: Q<sub>c</sub> = [B AB … A<sup>n−1</sup>B] is the controllability matrix; φ(A) = A<sup>n</sup> + a<sub>n−1</sub>A<sup>n−1</sup> + … + a<sub>0</sub>I is the desired polynomial with the matrix A substituted for s; the row [0 0 … 0 1] picks the last row of Q<sub>c</sub><sup>−1</sup>; K is 1 × n.

blocks.text: The matrix inverse exists only when Q<sub>c</sub> is nonsingular, which is the controllability test again. The formula assumes one input; with several inputs you solve the coefficient equations and may use the extra freedom for other goals.

figure.caption: Every state, not just the output, is multiplied by K and subtracted from the reference r, so the plant sees u = r − Kx and the closed-loop matrix becomes A − BK.

spec.title: State feedback
spec.aria: The gain K feeds every state back to the summing junction; the closed-loop matrix is A − BK.

examples.question: A plant has A = [[0, 1], [0, 0]] and B = [0, 1]<sup>T</sup>, with both states available for measurement. The control law is u = r − Kx, where K = [k<sub>1</sub> k<sub>2</sub>]. (a) Check that pole placement is possible. (b) Find K so that the closed-loop poles sit at −2 and −3. (c) Verify the result.
steps: Controllability: AB = A·B = [[0,1],[0,0]]·[0,1]<sup>T</sup> = [1, 0]<sup>T</sup>. So Q<sub>c</sub> = [B AB] = [[0,1],[1,0]]. det Q<sub>c</sub> = (0)(0) − (1)(1) = −1, which is not zero, so the rank is 2 and the system is controllable. Placement is allowed.
Desired polynomial: φ(s) = (s + 2)(s + 3) = s² + 5s + 6. Matching form s² + a<sub>1</sub>s + a<sub>0</sub> gives a<sub>1</sub> = 5 and a<sub>0</sub> = 6.
Form BK: BK = [0, 1]<sup>T</sup>[k<sub>1</sub> k<sub>2</sub>] = [[0, 0], [k<sub>1</sub>, k<sub>2</sub>]]. Therefore A − BK = [[0, 1], [−k<sub>1</sub>, −k<sub>2</sub>]].
Characteristic polynomial: det(sI − (A − BK)) = det[[s, −1], [k<sub>1</sub>, s + k<sub>2</sub>]] = s(s + k<sub>2</sub>) − (−1)(k<sub>1</sub>) = s² + k<sub>2</sub>s + k<sub>1</sub>.
Equate coefficients: the s coefficient gives k<sub>2</sub> = 5; the constant term gives k<sub>1</sub> = 6. Hence K = [6 5].

Verification: the roots of s² + 5s + 6 are s = (−5 ± √(25 − 24))/2 = (−5 ± 1)/2, that is −2 and −3. Both lie in the left half plane, so with r = 0 the state decays as a combination of e<sup>−2t</sup> and e<sup>−3t</sup>.
examples.answer: K = [6 5] places the closed-loop poles exactly at −2 and −3, as demanded.
examples.check:
import math
# desired polynomial (s+2)(s+3) = s^2 + 5s + 6
a2, a1, a0 = 1, 5, 6
# for A = [[0,1],[0,0]], B = [0,1]^T: det(sI-(A-BK)) = s^2 + k2*s + k1
k1 = a0
k2 = a1
print(k1)
print(k2)
disc = a1 * a1 - 4 * a2 * a0
print((-a1 + math.sqrt(disc)) / (2 * a2))
print((-a1 - math.sqrt(disc)) / (2 * a2))

traps: Sign of K: u = r − Kx gives A − BK. If you write u = r + Kx the closed-loop matrix is A + BK and every gain changes sign, so the same K places different poles.
Placing poles without testing controllability. If Q<sub>c</sub> is singular, no K exists and the coefficient equations contradict each other; the examiner looks for the rank check first.

Swapping the gains in a 2×2 problem. For A = [[0,1],[0,0]] the constant term of det(sI − (A − BK)) is k<sub>1</sub> and the s coefficient is k<sub>2</sub>; match the highest power first and work down.
Calling K a PID gain. K is a row of n gains, one per state; the P, PI and PID gains of Unit 5 act on the single error signal and cannot place n poles.
Forgetting that the law needs every state measured. If only y is available, K alone is not enough; an observer must estimate x first.

quiz.q: Write the closed-loop state equation obtained from x' = Ax + Bu with u = r − Kx.
quiz.a: x' = (A − BK)x + Br. The closed-loop matrix is A − BK and its eigenvalues are the closed-loop poles.

quiz.q: Why must the pair (A, B) be controllable before you attempt pole placement?
quiz.a: Controllability means the input can reach every state, so the n gains in K can influence all n modes. If the rank of Q<sub>c</sub> is less than n, some mode is untouched by u and its pole stays fixed whatever K you choose.

quiz.q: For A = [[0, 1], [−2, −3]] and B = [0, 1]<sup>T</sup>, find K = [k<sub>1</sub> k<sub>2</sub>] that places the closed-loop poles at −4 and −5.
quiz.a: BK = [[0,0],[k<sub>1</sub>,k<sub>2</sub>]], so A − BK = [[0,1],[−2−k<sub>1</sub>, −3−k<sub>2</sub>]]. det(sI − (A − BK)) = s² + (3 + k<sub>2</sub>)s + (2 + k<sub>1</sub>). Desired: (s+4)(s+5) = s² + 9s + 20. So 3 + k<sub>2</sub> = 9 gives k<sub>2</sub> = 6, and 2 + k<sub>1</sub> = 20 gives k<sub>1</sub> = 18. K = [18 6].

quiz.q: A design asks for closed-loop poles at −1 + j2 and −1 − j2. Write the desired characteristic polynomial.
quiz.a: φ(s) = (s + 1 − j2)(s + 1 + j2) = (s + 1)² + 4 = s² + 2s + 5. The coefficients are real because the poles are a conjugate pair.

quiz.q: A student uses u = r + Kx with the K = [6 5] found for the law u = r − Kx, on A = [[0,1],[0,0]], B = [0,1]<sup>T</sup>. Where do the closed-loop poles land, and what does it mean?
quiz.a: A + BK = [[0,1],[6,5]], so det(sI − (A + BK)) = s² − 5s − 6, roots s = 6 and s = −1. One pole is in the right half plane, so the closed loop is unstable. The sign of the feedback path matters more than the numbers.

quiz.q: State Ackermann's formula and name each term.
quiz.a: K = [0 0 … 0 1] Q<sub>c</sub><sup>−1</sup> φ(A), where Q<sub>c</sub> = [B AB … A<sup>n−1</sup>B] is the controllability matrix of the single-input system, φ(A) is the desired polynomial with A substituted for s, and the leading row selects the last row of the inverse.

quiz.q: State feedback with K and a cascade PID controller can both give the same closed-loop poles on one plant. Which design needs more sensors, and which is easier to retune when the plant changes?
quiz.a: State feedback needs all n states measured, so it needs more sensors or an observer; PID needs only the error y, so a single sensor. Retuning: PID gains are one to three numbers adjusted on site, while K is n numbers that must be recomputed from A and B when the model changes.

beyond: Not for the exam. Linear quadratic regulator design, in Unit 7, computes the best K automatically by minimising a cost on state error and control effort, so no polynomial matching is done by hand. When the states cannot all be measured, an observer such as a Luenberger or Kalman filter estimates them and K uses the estimates, and the separation principle lets the two designs be done independently. Search for 'Ackermann formula place acker', 'observer-based state feedback' and 'discrete-time pole placement' to continue.
